I work at an internal tech support/helpdesk and I've seen a few ways people mass quit or get let go...

  1. Lack of leadership - We had a supervisor get promoted to leadership and a stretch of 3+ months of no supervisor led to about 50% of the team quitting.
  2. Underpaid - If you can get paid more for doing a similar job you will not stay. The company hasn't raised their pay levels to meet the market at all. People quit and went to...
  3. Competing companies with high need - Competing, as in, for resources, not necessarily the exact same industry. If one person leaves to one of these companies they can (and will) take most of the team with them. They will also pay more, see point 2.
  4. Temporary reduced need - Many companies are short sighted and will fire people when there's a reduction in need then wonder why the people remaining can't handle the increased volume during a boom...which leads to...
  5. Burn out - Overtaxing your resources because of "cutting the fat" or "temporary boom" or whatever will cause your good people to straight up quit...leaving you with only the fat. Usually one bad decision of adding an extra layer of work to people who are already spread too thin will cause this type of hemorrhage.

In college I was in the work study program. I worked for the admissions department. Most work study jobs didn't involve very much work, but ours did. We were expected to make hundreds of phone calls to potential students. We would get in at around 5 and bust our asses making as many calls as quickly as possible. If we got enough done, collectively, we could leave early and still get paid for a four hour shift. That meant that I would basically work really hard from about 5-7 and then get paid $32 (5 to 9). That really worked for me. I preferred working really hard for 2 hours instead of just sitting on my ass for 4.

One day the director of the admissions department came down. We all knew something was up because everyone was required to come in that day, or we were fired. She accused us all of stealing, and said that by working two hours and then getting paid for four that we'd effectively stolen from the school. She said we would be required to work double hours, unpaid, until we earned back what we stole.

Our "managers" who were just grad students just stood there stupidly and accepted this, without defending us at all. So I spoke up. First, I explained that we didn't owe them anything and hadn't stolen anything because we completed the allotted four hours of work in two hours. I also explained that we worked considerably harder than everyone else in the work study program, but were paid the same. We only left when we were all collectively finished. I also pointed out that none of us knew that that wasn't the official policy. She responded that it didn't matter; from now on if we finished our work we could stay and do homework but we couldn't leave. She also said that if we could finish in two hours then they would be doubling our work load. This didn't make much sense because we were always caught up on our work. What she meant was she was going to create new work. She was being completely unreasonable. So I said so. I told her that what she was asking was totally unreasonable and that I know I speak for everyone when I say that. Her response: "fine, then your fired". So I asked everyone else "who else quits?" Everyone. Everyone quit right on the spot.

The next day, they hired everyone back. We all agreed that we wouldn't go back to work unless they agreed not to double the work and not to make us earn any hours back. They agreed. Under one condition, however. Everyone but me was hired back. Oh well, I still won.

So I worked on this helpdesk project at a Fortune 500 company. This is the story all about how that project got flip fucked up right round.

Our project was divided into two helpdesks, which had separate staff and supported separate applications but were for the same client. Everything was going well, people were generally happy despite the pay being below standard for a helpdesk job. This goes on for about 5 years or so when our project wins a bid and now has to support two additional helpdesks. Management decides that they will split the calls evenly between the two existing helpdesk staffs since both have around 20 minutes of free time per hour. This is where the domino effect of stupidity happens.

So the staff members receive piss poor training because this is all brand new, and being unable to handle calls effectively shoots up handle time 300% per agent. Now calls are constantly in queue because the volumes are much higher and so are the handle times. SLA is being missed, so the project beings suffering major revenue penalties and such. People are quitting faster than they can be hired. Management decides that they need to give everybody raises and OT to keep them from quitting, but they only way they can afford this is to lay off the top supervisor (who is essential to the project).

So the supervisor is now gone, leaving only 1 junior supervisor to manage 4 helpdesks, 3 of which he has no training on. Everybody gets raises, but now supervisor duties are being offloaded onto senior agents. Once again, the job is way overwhelming for the amount of pay, and the senior agents begin quitting. There are gaps in coverage everywhere, and turnover rate is still dangerously high. This goes on for about two years while the project misses SLA on each of its helpdesks pretty much every month. Finally the client gets fed up and gives 2 of the projects to another company instead.

So now the project is back where it started, except minus almost all of its senior staff, and paying everybody a lot more than it was before, so likely making a lot less profit. This is a perfect example of "If it isn't broken, don't fix it".

Intro: Options trading is highly speculative. If you know what you're doing and hedge your bets, you can make money. If you don't know what you're doing, you can lose unforeseeable amounts of money. Basically, you're betting on what a stock price will do without actually buying any stock.

To dumb it down to basics, say something costs $10. You think by October it will only be $8. You can 'sell' stock that you don't have for the $10 it is now, betting that it will only cost you $8 to buy back. If it goes all the way down to $0, you get to keep all your money. If, instead of going down to $8, it goes up to $1,000, you have to pay the $1,000 for however many you sold.

This is obviously very risky. When you try to do this at a brokerage, they make sure you have enough assets to screw around with and know what you're doing first.

When I worked at a brokerage, the team in charge of deciding who was allowed to trade options and how much risk they were allowed to take had ~6 people on it. One of them heard a "hot tip" from a client. They all approved each other for unlimited options trading, and sold a bunch of naked calls. The underlying stock rocketed and they, collectively, were out a couple hundred thousand dollars, which they obviously had no ability to pay back. The entire team got canned when it came out. I ran into one of them running a gas station a few months later.

I was sitting here at Scooter's Coffeehouse with my earbuds in and started wondering what others like to listen to when they write?
Are you all about the silence? Or are you rocking out to a heavy guitar riff? Maybe something a little more electronic is your thing. Either way, I was wanting to know what you lovely people like to listen to when you sit down to write?
What kind of music helps you write?

I was able to get through some frustrating edits listening to Taiwanese singers, Rainie Yang and Jolin Tsai. When I write, I don't usually listen to anything as I find it distracting. Although, in the past, I have tried to create soundtracks for stories.

Interesting. I understand that silence can definitely be helpful for most people. I have an annoying case of tinnitus, so silence isn't an option for me.
I've done the same with the soundtracks. I sometimes put on something with the same emotion I'm trying to portray.

For me it actually depends on what I'm writing. Generally I listen to fast paced and upbeat music when I write. I have a playlist dedicated to the stuff actually. But sometimes if I have to write a particularly sad scene or story I listen to more sombre and sad music. Music affects the way I feel which in turn affects the way I write too. I once wrote something that made me so sad I didn't publish it out of fear of it being criticized. That's probably too far.

I'm with you on the upbeat music. I personally like to listen to electronic music sometimes (DeadMau5 style) and I've found it helps with writing. Though I just want to say that you should never fear criticism. Criticism may hurt at the moment, but in the end it is fantastic for building your skills.

I personally listen to anything that fits the mood. I've found myself listening to DeadMau5 and Ellie Goulding for a few of my writing sessions (Upbeat, catchy tunes, etc.) But I'm also guilty of trying to build soundtracks for my stories. I one time found a song with the same title as my book, and the overall song had a similar story to my story (100% coincidence) and it pumped me up like crazy.
The biggest HOWEVER for me though is Editing. I absolutely cannot listen to anything with lyrics when I'm proofreading/editing. If I do it takes me forever to get through a single page. I don't know if it's an ADD thing, but reading words and having words pumped through my ears.... yeah, it doesn't work. I've moved to listening to house/electronic music for this, but also found that there are some really good string quartet bands out there that really help. A good example of this is the Vitamin String Quartet . They cover popular music in lyricless quartet format and it's amazing.
I can respect that. Trent alone is awesome.
